pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Gut Bacteria & Digestion

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion):** "the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No specific MS performance expectation on the gut microbiome; the beneficial-microbe idea sits loosely under matter cycling (MS-LS1-7 / ecosystem PEs). This is UK-led content. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children explain that the gut is home to a huge community of bacteria (the microbiome), that MANY of these bacteria are beneficial rather than harmful, and that they do jobs human enzymes cannot — notably fermenting/breaking down dietary fibre the body cannot digest alone, and helping maintain a healthy gut environment (and making some vitamins). They describe what may happen when the microbiome is disrupted (e.g. by antibiotics or poor diet). The move that matters is overturning the 'all bacteria are germs' idea: here bacteria are partners in a mutualistic relationship, extending the body's digestive capability.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on digestion & enzymes and on knowing unicellular organisms; a relatively modern, evidence-evolving topic. A child is secure when they can state one thing gut bacteria do that our own enzymes cannot, explain why that matters, and give a consequence of disrupting the microbiome.
bestPractices: Lead with the myth-correction — most gut bacteria are helpful partners, not germs — since this is the central conceptual shift.
Contrast what human enzymes CAN'T do (digest fibre) with what bacteria CAN, so the partnership is concrete.
Use the mutualism framing (both benefit) to connect to ecology/relationships between organisms.
Include disruption (antibiotics, poor diet) and its consequences so the microbiome's importance is felt.
Keep claims evidence-appropriate — the field is fast-moving; teach the well-established roles (fibre fermentation, gut health, some vitamin synthesis).
keyRepresentations: Gut scene showing the bacterial community in the large intestine
Two-track comparison: human enzymes vs bacterial fermentation on the same fibre
Mutualism diagram (bacteria get food/home; we get fibre broken down + gut health)
Before/after disruption panel (healthy diverse community vs depleted)
commonMisconceptions: Believing all bacteria are harmful germs, rather than mostly beneficial partners.
Thinking humans digest fibre themselves, rather than relying on gut bacteria to ferment it.
Assuming antibiotics only kill 'bad' bacteria and leave the helpful community untouched.
Thinking the microbiome is fixed rather than changing with diet.
Confusing gut bacteria with the pathogens that cause food poisoning.

learn.summary: For learners aged 12–13 (UK KS3 Biology: 'the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system'), the central goal is to overturn the 'all bacteria are germs' idea and understand the gut microbiome as a mostly beneficial, mutualistic community. Learners should name at least one thing gut bacteria do that human enzymes cannot (notably fermenting dietary fibre), explain why that matters, and give a consequence of disrupting the microbiome (e.g. by antibiotics or a fibre-poor diet). Guidance centres on an interactive 'tend the gut community' model that is proposed to make the partnership causal, supported by a reveal-based gut scene, an in-role scientist conversation for 'why' questions, and sorting/short-answer checks. Relative efficacy of these media is untested.

activities.title: Tend your gut community: two digestion tracks
feedback: If the learner feeds only low-fibre foods: point out the bacterial track has little to work on and gut health does not rise — highlight that fibre is the bacteria's fuel.
When the fibre slides untouched through the enzyme track: prompt 'Which track finally acts on this fibre, and what does that tell you about what your bacteria add?'
After the antibiotic/poor-diet crash: ask the learner to predict what a person might feel (e.g. upset stomach, diarrhoea) and why recovery depends on diversity returning.
Reinforce the myth-correction when it arises in play: most of these trillions of residents are helpful partners, not germs to be eliminated.
activities.rationale: The role of gut bacteria is a dynamic, ecological process; letting the learner act on the community and see consequences is proposed to make the mutualistic partnership causal rather than merely asserted, and may let the fragility and importance of the microbiome be experienced. Relative efficacy against other media is untested. Live recolouring, a rising/falling gut-health meter, food-selection controls and the parallel two-track comparison are offered as concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Feed a model gut by choosing foods: food first passes through the small intestine, where the body's own enzymes work, then reaches a model colon (large intestine) full of bacteria. Watch the two digestion tracks side by side.
Observe that the body's own enzymes break down starch, sugars and protein, but cannot digest dietary fibre. The fibre passes undigested through the small intestine into the large intestine.
Watch the bacterial community act on that same fibre, fermenting it, producing beneficial products, and raising a 'gut health' indicator.
Introduce a disruption — a course of antibiotics or a switch to a fibre-poor diet — and observe the community decline and gut health drop.

Restore fibre-rich foods and observe the model's gut health recover as bacterial diversity returns. In real people, recovery after antibiotics can be slow or incomplete, and it varies from person to person.
State in your own words why the two digestive systems complete each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Fibre, which the body's own enzymes cannot digest, is a major food source for the bacterial partners, so human enzymes and gut bacteria complement each other. The microbiome is mostly beneficial, and disrupting it can have real consequences for digestion.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap gut scene: name the roles, bust the myth
feedback: If the learner expects all reveals to say 'harmful', surface the contrast between a few disease-causing species and the many helpful residents.
Confirm correct naming: fibre fermentation is the headline role human enzymes cannot perform.
activities.rationale: A tap/lift-to-reveal scene is an efficient way to name roles and address the myth layer. It is a naming scaffold and does not itself show the ecological dynamics of feeding and disruption; the tap-to-reveal and flap panels are concrete interaction examples offered, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Tap the large-intestine community to reveal 'trillions of mostly helpful bacteria'.
Tap the fibre to reveal that bacteria ferment fibre that human enzymes cannot digest.
Open the flap 'Are gut bacteria harmful?' to reveal 'Most are helpful partners — we depend on them.'
Add a note of one further job (e.g. helping maintain a healthy gut environment or making some vitamins).
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can name what beneficial gut bacteria do and directly confront the 'all bacteria are harmful' idea.

activities.title: Ask the microbiome scientist (enrichment)
feedback: When a myth surfaces in a question, the scientist separates a few pathogens from the trillions of helpful residents rather than simply asserting the answer.
Keep claims evidence-appropriate: this is a fast-moving field, so emphasise well-established roles (fibre fermentation, gut health, some vitamin synthesis) and flag where science is still evolving.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role conversation can follow a learner's questions and address 'why' and myths Socratically. It is valuable for the reasoning and myth layer; a dialogue can support, and need not replace, an interactive model intended to make the ecological dynamics felt. The relative efficacy of these media is untested.
learnerActions: Pose your own 'why' questions to an in-role gut-microbiome scientist, e.g. 'Why does my diet change my gut bacteria?' or 'What do probiotics do?'
Follow up on answers about what the bacteria do, why fibre matters, and what disrupts them.
Summarise one thing you learned that changed or confirmed your earlier idea.
activities.intendedInsight: The microbiome is an active, curiosity-rich research area; learners can pursue open questions and have their own ideas named and probed through dialogue.

activities.title: Check it: roles, what bacteria digest, disruption consequences
feedback: Full response: explains the microbiome is mostly beneficial, does jobs (fibre fermentation, crowding out pathogens) our enzymes can't, and predicts consequences of disruption.
Partial response: accepts gut bacteria can be helpful but cannot specify what they do (fibre breakdown) or what disruption causes — prompt for a specific job.

Gap response: treats all bacteria as harmful germs; reteach by contrasting a few disease-causing species with the trillions of helpful residents and showing fibre left undigested when bacteria are lost.
activities.rationale: Beneficial-vs-harmful sorting and 'what bacteria do that our enzymes can't' are clean items for surfacing the target misconceptions and confirming the specific knowledge. Recognition/sorting formats check classification but do not by themselves elicit extended independent explanation; the diagnostic prompt is included to draw out reasoning.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Answer: 'What do gut bacteria digest that we cannot?' (Answer: dietary fibre.)
Match each disruption (e.g. broad-spectrum antibiotics, fibre-poor diet) to a likely consequence (e.g. impaired digestion, diarrhoea, loss of diversity).

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Adverts sell soap that kills 99.9% of all bacteria. Your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics killed many of them?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners demonstrate they can distinguish beneficial from harmful bacteria, identify fibre as what bacteria digest that we cannot, and predict consequences of disruption.

constraints: Lead with the myth-correction — most gut bacteria are helpful partners, not germs — as the central conceptual shift, and separate the few pathogens (e.g. food-poisoning species) from the resident microbiome.

Keep claims evidence-appropriate: the microbiome is a fast-moving research area; teach the well-established roles (fibre fermentation, maintaining gut health, synthesising some vitamins) and avoid overstating effects.
The reveal-based gut scene is a naming scaffold only; it does not demonstrate the feed/ferment/disrupt dynamics, so pair it with an interactive model or discussion for the causal story.
Sorting and multiple-choice items check recognition and recall; they do not by themselves require learners to construct an extended explanation, so include an open prompt for full-response reasoning.
The in-role scientist conversation is enrichment for 'why' questions; its answers should stay within established science and flag evolving areas rather than assert certainty.
Present the on-screen colon, tracks and meters as a model of real digestion, not a literal depiction; actual timings, populations and recovery vary by person, diet and medication.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (British Nutrition Foundation, dietary fibre and gut bacteria) is marked verified:false in the row; the specific claims about vitamin synthesis and antibiotic-driven disruption rest on it and should be confirmed before being presented as settled fact.

The source row's '3D adds nothing' judgement for this topic was not carried over as a universal claim; it reflects a fit ranking, not established comparative efficacy. 3D was simply not proposed because the content is relational rather than spatial.

The original framing that the live model makes the partnership 'causal rather than asserted' and that other media cannot make dynamics 'felt' is a design preference, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; efficacy wording in the activity rationales has been softened to proposed/may/intended language accordingly.
The enrichment conversation activity carries no sourceClaims because its rationale concerns the dialogue medium (untested efficacy) rather than a factual claim the source substantiates.

NGSS has no specific middle-school performance expectation for the gut microbiome (the idea sits loosely under matter cycling / MS-LS1-7); this is UK-led content, which may affect portability to US contexts.

probeDeeper: If bacteria were all harmful, why would getting rid of your gut bacteria make your digestion worse, not better?
What can your gut bacteria do to your food that your own digestive enzymes cannot?
Why might someone get an upset stomach during a course of antibiotics?
How is a helpful gut bacterium different from a bacterium that causes food poisoning?
assess.correctAnswer: The gut bacteria are largely beneficial (a mutualistic microbiome): they break down dietary fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest and help keep harmful microbes out. Wiping them out — for example with broad-spectrum antibiotics — can disrupt digestion, cause diarrhoea, and let harmful species take over until the microbiome recovers.

errorPatterns.pattern: All bacteria are germs that make you ill
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate pathogens from the beneficial microbiome; most gut bacteria help us. Contrast a few disease-causing species with the trillions of helpful residents.
errorPatterns.distractor: The gut bacteria are germs — you'd be healthier if you killed them all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the gut bacteria are harmful and you'd be healthier without them

errorPatterns.pattern: The human gut could digest everything on its own, without bacteria
errorPatterns.nextMove: Humans can't digest much dietary fibre; gut bacteria ferment it, releasing useful products. Their loss leaves fibre undigested.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims human enzymes handle all food, so bacteria are unnecessary

errorPatterns.pattern: The gut bacteria are an infection you caught
errorPatterns.nextMove: The microbiome is a resident community built up from birth and normally kept in balance, not an infection.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the microbiome as invaders that got in, rather than resident partners

responseLevels.gap: Treats all bacteria as harmful germs; sees no useful role for microbes in the gut.
responseLevels.full: Explains the microbiome is mostly beneficial, does jobs (fibre fermentation, crowding out pathogens) our enzymes can't, and predicts the consequences of disrupting it.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that gut bacteria can be helpful but cannot say specifically what they do (fibre breakdown) or what disruption causes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Adverts sell soap that 'kills 99.9% of all bacteria' as if every microbe is the enemy. But your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics wiped them out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the microbiome sees these bacteria as helpful partners with a digestive job. A child holding 'all bacteria are germs' treats them as invaders that should be destroyed and cannot explain why losing them harms digestion.
